item.title: Citrix NetScaler vulnerability (CVE-2026-88779) in active exploitation
item.description:
On October 4, 2026, Citrix disclosed a high-severity (CVSS score of 8.7) memory overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-88779) affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway deployments that are configured as either a SAML Service Provider (SP) or SAML Identity Provider (IdP). Successful exploitation can cause a denial of service (DoS) condition, potentially disrupting authentication services and remote access functionality. This vulnerability affects customer-managed Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances. Citrix-managed cloud services and Citrix-managed Adaptive Authentication services are not affected, as the required updates are applied to those platforms.

Active exploitation has been reported. Citrix has observed targeted attacks against unpatched NetScaler deployments, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added CVE-2026-88779 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog.

Recommended actions

Counter Threat Unit™ (CTU) researchers recommend that organizations identify affected systems and apply the latest Citrix security updates as soon as possible as appropriate to minimize the risk of service disruption. Organizations should prioritize internet-facing and business-critical deployments.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this vulnerability and will deliver detections and protections as available.

item.title: Understanding Asymmetric Routing Risks in Modern Firewall Deployments
item.description:
In modern network environments, maintaining both operational efficiency and strong security controls requires careful design and planning. One of the more common challenges Sophos Professional Services encounters, especially during firewall upgrades or redesigns, is asymmetric routing.


What Is Asymmetric Routing?

Asymmetric routing occurs when the outbound and return traffic of a single connection take different network paths. In these scenarios, data sent from a client to a server may follow one path, while the return traffic takes a completely different route.  Legacy stateless firewalls may permit this behavior, but it introduces potential security and inspection gaps that become increasingly problematic in modern security architectures.


How Asymmetric Routing Increases AiTM Risk

Asymmetric routing can introduce conditions that increase the risk of adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks. An AiTM attack (sometimes referred to as man-in-the-middle or MitM) occurs when an attacker positions themselves between two communicating parties to intercept or modify traffic without detection. When traffic flows along different paths, security devices such as firewalls may only observe part of the communication. This creates blind spots in inspection and validation.

Consider the following scenarios:

  • Uneven inspection paths: A client request passes through a firewall and is inspected, but the response returns via a different device that does not enforce security controls.
  • Alternate path exposure: Traffic routed over secondary WAN links, MPLS circuits, or misconfigured devices may traverse infrastructure that is less secure, allowing attackers to intercept communications.
  • Traffic redirection attacks: Attackers may exploit routing weaknesses to position themselves “on path,” intercepting and relaying traffic while appearing transparent to both endpoints. 
  • Session manipulation: Because asymmetric routing can break session validation, attackers may inject or modify responses, potentially altering data in transit.

These conditions undermine both the integrity and confidentiality of communications, making it easier for attackers to observe or manipulate data.


Why Modern Firewalls Require Symmetry

Modern next-generation firewalls (NGFW) operate as stateful inspection devices. This means they must see both directions of a communication flow to properly establish and maintain session state.  Stateful firewalls track each connection and allow return traffic only when it matches a known session, preventing unauthorized responses or unsolicited traffic.

When asymmetric routing is present:

  • The firewall may only see one side of the session
  • Return traffic may be interpreted as invalid
  • Packets may be dropped due to missing session state

This behavior often leads to application failures, connectivity issues, and inconsistent performance.  Our team has seen firewall cutovers run long because of asymmetric routing, with serious consequences such as customers losing access to payroll systems on payday.


The Operational Impact of Introducing NGFWs

When an NGFW is introduced into an environment that previously allowed asymmetric routing, organizations commonly experience unexpected disruptions.  This is not a failure of the firewall, it is the result of enforcing proper security standards. What once appeared to “work” under less strict conditions is now blocked due to incomplete session visibility.  It can be tempting to resolve these disruptions by relaxing or bypassing stateful inspection for the affected traffic. While this may restore connectivity, it reopens the same inspection gaps described above. Treat it as a short-term workaround at most, not a fix.

Resolving these issues requires:

  • Identifying the source of asymmetric routing
  • Normalizing traffic paths
  • Ensuring both inbound and outbound traffic traverse the same inspection point


Common Causes of Asymmetric Routing

Asymmetric routing can arise from several common misconfigurations or design choices:

  • Misconfigured subnet masks
  • Incorrect default gateway settings on endpoints
  • Conflicting or invalid routing entries
  • Policy-based routing or SD-WAN configurations
  • Improper VLAN or Layer 2/Layer 3 design

In many enterprise designs, factors such as load balancing, redundancy, and multiple ISP connections naturally introduce the possibility of asymmetric paths.


The Hidden Risk: Business-Driven Network Design

A critical but often overlooked factor is how network architecture is originally designed.  Designing a network purely around business or operational needs, such as maximizing uptime, reducing costs, or optimizing traffic paths, without integrating security as a core requirement can introduce significant risk.

For example:

  • Multi-path routing for redundancy may unintentionally create asymmetric flows
  • Traffic offloading strategies may bypass inspection points
  • Cost-driven designs may rely on less secure network segments

Industry best practices emphasize the need to balance performance, cost, and security throughout the design process.  Ideally, security is incorporated from the beginning rather than retrofitted into an existing design. When that isn’t possible, such as during a firewall migration, validating traffic paths before cutover is essential. Frameworks such as Zero Trust and secure-by-design principles stress that security controls and visibility must be consistently applied across all traffic paths. 


Best Practice: Aligning Security with Network Design

The most effective network designs align business requirements with security architecture rather than treating them as competing priorities.

Key principles include:

  • Ensuring symmetric routing through security enforcement points
  • Centralizing inspection and control wherever possible
  • Avoiding designs that allow traffic to bypass firewalls
  • Validating routing behavior during design and testing phases


Conclusion

Asymmetric routing is not inherently a flaw; it is a natural outcome of complex network environments. However, when combined with modern stateful firewalls and security expectations, it introduces both operational challenges and security risks.  More importantly, it can create conditions that enable AiTM-style attacks by reducing visibility and control over network traffic.

Organizations deploying next-generation firewalls must take a holistic approach:

  • Design networks with both business and security requirements in mind
  • Eliminate or control asymmetric paths
  • Ensure consistent inspection and policy enforcement

By doing so, they can prevent disruptions, maintain a strong security posture, and fully realize the benefits of modern firewall technologies.

Planning a firewall migration or network redesign? Sophos Professional Services can help you identify asymmetric paths and validate traffic flows before cutover, so you can minimize disruption and avoid inspection gaps.

item.title: CISA’s 17 Common Active Directory Compromise Techniques: A Sophos MDR Perspective
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

A faster detection engine won’t help if the front door is still unlocked. Sophos’ 2025 Active Adversary Report found that attackers’ first attempt to breach Active Directory came within a median of 11 hours.

This article groups the 17 techniques identified by CISA and its government partners into four categories, showing how strong identity controls, useful telemetry, and MDR-led response work together when attackers abuse legitimate identity systems.

That urgency isn’t happening in a vacuum: AI is here to stay. Pandora’s box is open, and governments, companies leading the frontier models, and the cybersecurity industry are working together to establish responsible guardrails for how this technology is developed and used.

The practical reality for security teams is already here: AI is accelerating both defense and offense. Organizations can analyze data, investigate threats, and respond faster. Attackers can automate reconnaissance, generate tooling, and compress the time between initial access and impact. The Sophos AI Security 2026 Report makes the point: AI is compressing attack timelines, not inventing new attack types.

That acceleration makes identity fundamentals even more important. Microsoft Active Directory and Entra ID sit at the center of many on-premises and cloud environments, and attackers know that legitimate identity functions can take them from a foothold to privileged access.

As noted above, Sophos’ 2025 Active Adversary Report puts the median time between an attacker’s initial action and their first attempt to breach AD at just 11 hours — and AI may make that window smaller.

Rather than cover each of CISA’s 17 techniques individually, this review examines them through those four categories — the fundamentals defenders can apply, the telemetry that makes abuse visible, and how Sophos MDR helps detect, investigate, and respond.

The future of security will be increasingly agent-enabled, but the fundamentals remain nonnegotiable, and the four categories below start where most compromises still begin: credential access.

1. Credential access: Secure identities before attackers can use them

Techniques covered: Password spraying, Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, and passwords in Group Policy Preferences.

Credential-access techniques turn ordinary identity functions into a route toward broader access. A password spray, a Kerberos service-ticket request, or a legacy credential becomes more concerning when it connects to discovery and movement on the endpoint or in the network.

The fundamental controls include:

  • Use phishing-resistant MFA for privileged users.
  • Eliminate unnecessary service accounts.
  • Use group Managed Service Accounts where possible.
  • Remove legacy credentials.
  • Ensure authentication events are centrally logged.

A recent Sophos Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) engagement shows how quickly this can develop. In March 2026, Sophos investigated an Interlock ransomware incident in which the attacker queried Active Directory for domain-group information and then queried service principal names, indicating a Kerberoasting attempt.

The activity was not an isolated event. It was part of a broader sequence that began with an endpoint compromise and progressed into domain discovery, credential access, and lateral movement activity.

MDR takeaway: Sophos MDR can correlate authentication activity with endpoint and directory signals, then investigate when the combined pattern points to credential abuse. The point is not to treat every Kerberos request as malicious; it is to determine when identity activity is contributing to an attack sequence and support timely response.

Why this matters: Credential attacks can look like normal authentication activity. In the Interlock investigation, the attacker used familiar tools and legitimate protocols. Strong fundamentals, complete endpoint coverage, appropriate authentication controls, and useful telemetry give defenders more opportunities to identify and interrupt the attack earlier.

How Sophos can help: Sophos MDR connects Microsoft identity, endpoint, and directory signals to help determine when authentication activity is part of a broader attack sequence. Sophos ITDR can add identity posture checks, leaked-credential monitoring, and identity-specific response capabilities where organizations need deeper identity visibility.

2. Privilege escalation and lateral movement: Protect the paths to Tier 0

Techniques covered: MachineAccountQuota compromise, unconstrained delegation, DCSync, dumping ntds.dit, and Shadow Credentials.

Once attackers obtain an initial identity, they look for ways to increase their access. They may create a new computer account, abuse delegation, replicate directory data, or modify sensitive attributes to move closer to domain administrator privileges.

The fundamental controls include:

  • Restrict who can create computer accounts.
  • Eliminate unnecessary delegation.
  • Minimize replication permissions.
  • Protect domain controllers.
  • Review access to sensitive directory attributes.

A Sophos MDR case documented in the 2025 Active Adversary Report shows why the path to Tier 0 deserves its own discussion. After initial access through an unpatched FortiGate VPN appliance, the attacker moved laterally to a domain controller, used AV-killer tools, performed enumeration, and established persistence on multiple devices. Sophos MDR disrupted the activity while the attack was still unfolding.

MDR takeaway: Put privileged access and directory changes under continuous monitoring. Sophos MDR can investigate account and computer-object creation, explicit-credential logons, privileged operations, directory changes, and replication activity alongside the originating account, source system, and related endpoint behavior when that telemetry is available.

Why this matters: Many of these actions can be legitimate. A new computer account, directory modification, or replication request becomes meaningful when considered alongside the account that made it, the source system, related logons, and activity on the target system. MDR helps evaluate those connections instead of treating every administrative event as malicious.

How Sophos can help: Sophos MDR helps investigate the activity surrounding privilege escalation, including unusual logons, new or modified computer objects, privileged operations, and related endpoint behavior. Sophos ITDR can add visibility into risky permissions and identity relationships that may expose paths toward Tier 0.

3. Certificates and authentication: Protect the systems that issue trust

Techniques covered: AD CS compromise, including Golden Certificate, Golden Ticket, and Silver Ticket.

Trust is issued by infrastructure. Certificate authorities, certificate templates, domain controllers, and Kerberos services decide which credentials appear valid. That makes changes to the systems that issue trust as important as the authentication events that follow them.

The fundamental controls include:

  • Secure certificate templates.
  • Restrict access to certificate authorities and domain controllers.
  • Protect certificate private keys and backups.
  • Remove unnecessary authentication permissions.
  • Use group Managed Service Accounts where appropriate.
  • Maintain rotation and recovery procedures for critical Kerberos and computer-account secrets.

Recent Sophos research on the STAC4749 campaign shows why trust infrastructure deserves attention. In several incidents, attackers used embedded certificate-authority certificates to pin their command-and-control communications, making the connection appear trusted to the malware. This was not an AD CS compromise, but it illustrates the underlying problem: certificate trust can be abused below the visible sign-in event.

Sophos’ 2026 reporting reinforces the same lesson from a different angle: it identifies Golden Ticket attacks as a high-impact identity threat and emphasizes correlating endpoint, identity, and network telemetry when investigating privilege escalation and lateral movement.

MDR takeaway: Monitor the systems that issue trust, not only the authentications that follow. Sophos MDR can investigate certificate requests and issuance, changes to certificate templates or CA security settings, unusual Kerberos ticket activity, and related PowerShell or process activity on certificate authorities and domain controllers when that telemetry is enabled and available.

Why this matters: A forged certificate or Kerberos ticket may look like a valid authentication event. The more useful signal may be the activity around it: a certificate-template change followed by a certificate request, unexpected administration on a certificate authority, and unusual commands on a domain controller. Centralized logging and correlation give defenders more opportunities to identify that sequence.

How Sophos can help: Sophos Next-Gen SIEM can bring additional certificate, authentication, and legacy-system telemetry into the investigation workflow used by Sophos MDR, where those sources are configured and available. That broader history helps analysts investigate suspicious trust and authentication activity.

4. Persistence and hybrid coverage: Assume one reset may not be enough

Techniques covered: Golden SAML, Microsoft Entra Connect compromise, one-way domain trust bypass, SID History compromise, and Skeleton Key.

The more an environment depends on connected identity systems, the more response has to account for those connections. A compromised credential, token, trust, synchronization path, or authentication component can keep the attacker’s access alive after the first artifact is removed.

In March 2025, a Sophos employee fell victim to a phishing attack that captured credentials and bypassed MFA. The attacker tried to move into Sophos’ network, but Sophos Labs, Managed Detection and Response, Internal Detection and Response, and IT teams shared telemetry and investigated the activity. The incident is not one of CISA’s named AD techniques; it demonstrates the response principle behind this category: identity recovery must account for more than the first compromised password.

Sophos’ 2026 reporting reinforces the same point. Sixty-seven percent of the intrusions studied began with compromised credentials or other identity-related tactics, including authentication-token theft and abused trusted relationships.

The fundamental controls include:

  • Protect Microsoft Entra Connect, AD FS, and domain controllers as Tier 0 systems.
  • Separate privileged AD and Entra ID accounts.
  • Restrict trust relationships.
  • Review SID History.
  • Harden LSASS and domain controllers.
  • Centrally log synchronization, federation, authentication, and administrative activity.

MDR takeaway: When identity activity is suspicious, investigate the surrounding sessions, endpoints, directory changes, and connected Microsoft 365 activity before closing the case. Sophos MDR’s Microsoft integrations can provide that operating context and, where authorized, support actions such as blocking sign-in or revoking sessions. Sophos ITDR can add ongoing visibility into identity posture and relationships across AD and Entra ID.

Why this matters: The response to a compromised Microsoft 365 identity may involve resetting credentials, terminating Entra ID tokens, revoking sessions, removing malicious inbox rules, or disabling an unauthorized application. The same principle applies to Active Directory: removing the initial artifact is one step. Defenders must also validate the underlying trust relationships, credentials, tokens, and authentication systems for persistent access.

How Sophos can help: Sophos MDR can support authorized Microsoft 365 response actions, such as blocking sign-in or revoking sessions, while giving analysts context across sign-ins, endpoints, and related users. Sophos ITDR can add ongoing visibility into identity posture and AD/Entra ID relationships that may need review during recovery.

Conclusion

CISA’s 17 techniques point back to the same operational question: when an attacker starts using legitimate identity functions, can the organization see the sequence and act before it reaches Tier 0?

The answer still depends on fundamentals: protected privileged access, hardened identity systems, useful telemetry, and response actions that are ready to use. AI can make MDR faster and more scalable, but it cannot lock the front door.

That foundation remains the organization’s first defense against a shrinking 11-hour window.

item.title: Sophos AI Defense is now generally available
item.description:
When we introduced Sophos AI Defense in July, we focused on a challenge facing organizations everywhere: 

AI adoption is accelerating, often faster than security and IT teams can see or control it. New AI tools, embedded capabilities, and shadow AI are creating blind spots around where AI is being used and what information it can access.

Starting today, Sophos AI Defense is generally available, giving organizations the visibility and control to discover AI use, understand risk, apply guardrails, and protect sensitive information. Powered by Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-Native Cybersecurity Defense System, it brings AI security into the environment Sophos customers already use, rather than requiring another disconnected platform to manage. 

See AI. Control AI. Secure AI.

AI is increasingly embedded in the tools people use every day. That can create blind spots when employees adopt AI services that security teams do not know about or when AI functionality appears within applications already in use.

Sophos AI Defense helps bring that activity into view and gives security teams the context and controls to act:

  • See AI: Discover AI tools, agents, and workflows across your environment, including shadow AI.
  • Control AI: Apply practical guardrails for how AI can be used.
  • Secure AI: Protect sensitive information from AI-driven risk. 

Together, these capabilities help organizations move beyond simply knowing AI is being used to making informed decisions about how it should be used.

item.title: AI governance needs more than a policy document
item.description:
AI tools have made it remarkably easy for a company to expose its own data:  

  • An employee pastes a customer list into a chatbot to reformat it. 
  • A developer drops proprietary code into an assistant to debug it. 
  • Someone connects a new AI product to their work account to save a few hours a week. 

None of these actions seem malicious, but each one moves sensitive information somewhere the security team cannot see. 

This new era of "move fast and break things”, a phrase famously coined by Mark Zuckerberg in the early Facebook days, benefits attackers. Company data now flows through more places, more third parties, and more delegated credentials. 

Shadow AI is already widespread:

  • 82% of organizations have discovered at least one AI tool or workflow that security and IT did not know existed.
  • 90% of IT leaders say they are concerned about shadow AI from a privacy and security standpoint.

Organizations know this is a problem and will enact an AI policy to educate employees about acceptable AI use and satisfy compliance requirements. The assumption is that if employees know the rules, they will follow them. Unfortunately, governance does not work that way.  

An policy document and employee training are just the beginning of an AI governance strategy. AI policy only works when it’s backed by visibility and technical controls enforced within user workflows.

A real-world shadow AI-driven incident

In April 2026, Vercel disclosed that an attacker had reached internal systems through a third-party AI tool. Here’s what happened:

An employee signed up for a consumer AI product using their corporate Google Workspace account.

  • That employee granted broad permissions during self-service signup.
  • That vendor was breached months later.
  • The attacker used the stolen OAuth token to take over the Workspace account and reach sensitive company environments.

The risk wasn't the AI tool itself. It was the absence of controls around how it connected to corporate accounts.

The problem: Policies buckle under delivery pressure

The instinct after an incident like this is to reinforce policy more frequently. But the evidence tells a different story:

AI adoption follows the same pattern. When policy becomes a barrier to productivity, productivity will win.

Control pointWhat it observesWhat it can enforce

  • Non-browser activity

    • Redirects to approved alternatives
    • An exception path people can find

item.description:
Most people picture a cyberattack as something loud: files encrypting, screens locking, a ransom note. But the attacks that do real damage usually start quietly. 

Before an attacker steals data or deploys ransomware, they try to make sure nobody is watching. That means dealing with the endpoint protection on the device first.

The tools built for this job have a blunt name in the security industry: EDR Killers. Understanding how they work, and why they are harder to stop than they sound, explains a lot about what effective protection needs to do.

Why do attackers go after your endpoint protection?

Modern endpoint protection performs two high-level jobs. It blocks attacks it recognizes, and it records what happens on the device so suspicious behavior can be detected and investigated. That second job is called endpoint detection and response (EDR).

Both get in an attacker's way. If the protection is running, the exploit technique or the ransomware gets blocked. If the recording is running, the intrusion gets noticed. 

So, attackers treat security software the way a burglar treats a security camera: they deal with it before doing anything else. A common early step in a hands-on intrusion is to weaken or shut down the security software, then carry on with the real attack while the device is blind.

An EDR Killer is any tool built for that purpose. Some are malware written for the job. Others are repurposed legitimate software. Sophos X-Ops has seen the same EDR Killer, rebuilt for each attack, used ahead of ransomware from several competing groups. They all share the same goal: switch off the defenses, then proceed.

Bring your own vulnerable driver

Endpoint protection runs with high privileges, so an ordinary process cannot simply terminate it. To do that, an attacker needs help from the Windows kernel, the most privileged level of the operating system.

One of the most common ways to get that help is a technique called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD). A driver is a small piece of software that lets Windows communicate with hardware or other low-level components, and drivers run inside the kernel. Windows only loads drivers that have been digitally signed by a trusted publisher. The problem is that some legitimately signed drivers, often older ones, contain vulnerabilities that let whoever loads them do far more than the driver was designed for.

The attacker does not need to break the rules. They bring a real, signed, trusted driver along with them, install it on the victim's device, and then use its vulnerability to make the driver act on their behalf. Because the driver runs in the kernel, it can do what an ordinary process cannot, such as forcibly closing the endpoint protection processes. The driver is not malware. It is a legitimate component being used for an illegitimate purpose, so tools that look for malicious files have nothing to find.

What good protection looks like

A single defense against EDR Killers is not enough, because attackers have more than one way in. Protection must cover the attack from several angles at once.

Many EDR Killers, and the drivers they rely on, are already known, and reputation-based protection should stop them on sight. A driver known to be exploitable should be blocked outright, by default, because there is rarely a good reason to let it load. That block should not depend on the attack unfolding in one specific sequence first.

Attackers also change their tools, so protection must judge behavior as well as identity. How a program interacts with a driver, and what else is happening on the device at the time, should count as much as which driver it is.

Not every EDR Killer needs a vulnerable driver, either. Some borrow the signed drivers that ship with legitimate security testing tools, and some leave the protection running and attack the recording instead. Protection must cover those routes as well.

A determined attacker who is blocked once will try again. Protection should respond to repeated attempts by tightening its defenses, rather than waiting for the next move. 

Finally, protection against the attacker's end goal, such as ransomware, should run independently of the processes EDR Killers target. That way, it keeps working even if an attacker gets further than they should.

How Sophos Endpoint stops EDR Killers

Sophos Endpoint uses several complementary layers of defense against EDR Killers, each covering a different point in the attack.

The first line of defense deals with what Sophos has already seen. Reputation-based protection blocks known EDR Killer tools and suspicious files, drawing on threat intelligence gathered across the 300,000+ organizations using Sophos Endpoint worldwide. Known vulnerable drivers are blocked too, through a "Block vulnerable drivers" policy setting in Sophos Endpoint that is enabled by default on every protected device. The driver itself is the signal, so it is blocked before it can be used against Sophos Endpoint, whatever sequence the attack follows.

This works because of something attackers cannot easily change. A vulnerable driver must be legitimately signed to load at all, so the attacker cannot modify the file without breaking the signature. Its unique fingerprint (a cryptographic hash) stays the same, whatever the attacker renames it to. Sophos X-Ops threat intelligence keeps expanding the list of blocked drivers as new research and customer investigations confirm them, and the updates reach customers without a product update. If a particular driver is needed for legitimate business reasons, administrators can authorize it.

A vulnerable driver is not dangerous on its own. It only becomes useful to an attacker when something starts giving it orders. That usually happens through a standard Windows interface, and it is the point at which the attack becomes visible. Sophos Endpoint watches for exactly that pattern. A process that installs a driver and immediately begins sending it commands is behaving suspiciously, and Sophos weighs that against what else it knows about the process: where it came from, where it is running from, and what else it has been doing. An attempt to turn a signed driver against your endpoint protection is judged by what it is trying to do, not just by which driver it happens to be using. That matters, because the attacker can always bring a different driver. Tamper Protection adds kernel-level self-defense against EDR Killers that use vulnerable drivers.

Vulnerable drivers are not the only drivers attackers borrow. Some legitimate penetration-testing tools ship with their own signed drivers, and attackers misuse those drivers in the same way. A companion setting, "Block security tool drivers", stops them on the same principle: the driver is known, its fingerprint cannot change, and it is blocked before it loads. Tamper Protection gives Sophos Endpoint kernel-level self-defense against EDR Killers that use vulnerable drivers.

Sophos Endpoint also watches how programs use drivers, evaluating that activity against everything else happening on the device, so attempts to turn a signed driver against the security software are judged by their behavior, not only by the driver's identity.

Not every attempt to blind a device goes through a driver. Some attackers leave the protection running and go after the recording instead, tampering with Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), the stream of events that Windows produces and that security software, Sophos Endpoint included, relies on to see what is happening. The "Prevent ETW tampering" setting in Sophos Endpoint blocks those attempts, so the device keeps reporting while it is under attack.

When an attacker keeps trying, protection tightens. Repeated EDR Killer behavior is one of the signals that automatically switches on Adaptive Attack Protection, which enables stricter defenses on that device while the attack is underway. And CryptoGuard, the Sophos Endpoint ransomware protection, runs as a filter driver inside the kernel, separate from the endpoint protection processes EDR Killers typically attempt to terminate. Even an attacker who gets past the earlier layers cannot reliably encrypt data. In 2024, attackers behind an attempted RansomHub attack tried to switch off Sophos protection with an EDR Killer called EDRKillShifter. The tool failed, and the ransomware they ran next failed when it triggered CryptoGuard.

Some organizations want to go further on devices that rarely change, such as domain controllers and other servers. For those devices, Sophos Endpoint offers a setting called "Detect new kernel drivers." When it is enabled, every new kernel driver installed on the device is recorded as an event, and administrators can combine those events with custom detection rules to raise an alert or open a case, such as a high-severity case whenever a new driver appears on a domain controller. The setting is off by default, because on an everyday workstation new drivers are routine and the events would be noise. On a device that should not change, a new driver is worth a look.

What this looks like in practice: seven attempts, seven blocks

A recent incident at a Sophos customer shows the layers working together.

An attacker tried to load a legitimately signed but vulnerable driver on a protected device. When the load was blocked, they renamed the file to look like a normal Windows component and tried again and again. Over 76 minutes, the same driver was presented under seven different Windows-like filenames.

Every attempt was blocked. The filename changed seven times, but the driver’s fingerprint never did, so the default-on policy caught each one.

The repeated attempts contributed to Adaptive Attack Protection switching on automatically for the device. When the attacker later tried a different approach, using a registry change to disable Microsoft Defender, that was blocked too.

The vulnerable driver never loaded. After a final round of reconnaissance, no further malicious activity was observed on the device.

Conclusion

Attackers go after security software first because everything else they want to do depends on nobody watching. Sophos Endpoint is built with that in mind: known tools are stopped on sight, known vulnerable drivers and the drivers that ship with penetration-testing tools are blocked, driver abuse is judged by its behavior, the recording the various protection products depend on is guarded, defenses tighten when an attack persists, and the protection that matters most runs separately from what EDR Killers target. Organizations that want a stricter posture on servers can flag every new driver that appears.

If you are evaluating endpoint protection, ask your vendor how they handle a legitimately signed driver being used against you. 

To learn more about Sophos Endpoint and start a free trial, visit sophos.com/endpoint.

item.title: Building intent-based access control without reading minds
item.description:
In Minority Report, the Department of Precrime promised certainty. Three precognitives saw the future, the system picked the consensus, and police arrested people for murders they hadn't yet committed. The whole machine depended on one buried secret: sometimes the precogs disagreed, and the dissenting vision, the minority report, was quietly deleted. The system held together as long as the precogs agreed, but broke when it removed its own doubt.

A new wave of security products is reaching for the same capability. The pitch goes something like this: put a small AI model on every laptop, let it watch what people do across their apps, browsers, and AI tools the way a colleague sitting behind them would, understand what each person is trying to do, determine if they are malicious, and intervene before the damage is done. The same monitoring keeps a complete record of work, so an analyst can read what happened instead of piecing it together from scattered logs. The person might be an employee pasting sensitive data into an unapproved AI assistant, an outsider logged in with stolen credentials, or someone following a scammer's instructions to hand over remote control of their laptop. The watching part is now straightforward with local models. The design question is what a system should do with inference about intent that won’t always be correct.

Strip away the architecture and the pitch makes three promises: catch a risky action in time to stop it, tell it apart from normal work without burying analysts in alerts, and make whatever gets flagged quick to investigate. Useful intent-based access control can be built today by combining contextual inference with explicit policy and enforcement at sensitive actions. The research supports reconstructing what happened after the fact, scoring how well an action fits a person's job, and adding friction at the moment of risk. Recognizing someone's immediate goal while they're still pursuing it is less settled, and reliably separating malicious from benign motives in ordinary work is a challenge. So working systems test something more concrete: how well an action fits the person's job, how unusual it is for them, or which objective on a short list it matches. Each test trades false alarms for misses differently, and each leaves a gap an imitator can hide in, which is why the design around the test matters as much as the test itself. We’ll start with what a local model can read from the screen, move through the tests from most to least concrete, take the case where the intent belongs to someone else, and finish with how the tests combine into access control.

What a local model can read from the screen

Reconstructing what someone did on their screen already works surprisingly well. Cohen et al. split the job in two. A small model first summarizes each step of a short UI trajectory, using screenshots and action records to capture what was on screen and what the user did, and a second fine-tuned model infers the goal from those summaries. With Gemini Flash 8B as the small model, that decomposed pipeline inferred the user's goal about as well as Gemini 1.5 Pro, a model that cost more than 30 times as much per token. Jiang et al.'s task-induction method handles an earlier step, sorting interleaved computer-use traces back into their original tasks with near-perfect agreement.

Both results are retrospective. Each settles its answer after the last interaction, which suits post-incident response but doesn't establish how reliably a goal can be identified while someone is still pursuing it.

Established endpoint vendors and newer products alike are building around small, specialized models that make decisions in real time, in some cases directly on the device. Many rely mainly on structured events such as clipboard copies, file access, browser content, data lineage, and a baseline of each person's normal work. Some capture screenshots around an incident as evidence rather than continuously interpreting the screen, and that’s a reasonable choice: evidence that makes an alert quick to check lowers the cost of every false alarm. Logins, file access, process launches, and payment events arrive already labeled, so there's little left to summarize, and none of the studies reviewed here measures the added security value of reading the screen on top of those event streams.

The harder problem is inferring the goal mid-session from only the evidence available so far. GUIDE, a CVPR 2026 benchmark built from 67.5 hours of novice users working in apps like Photoshop and Excel, took a first step. It cut clips averaging about 25 seconds off at 25%, 50%, and 75% and asked models to pick the user's immediate goal from four options. With a quarter of the clip, the best model in this partial-clip experiment picked correctly about half the time, rising to about two thirds with the full clip, where random guessing gets 25%. Even with the overall task and possible immediate goals supplied, models frequently chose the wrong one. The researchers used users’ spoken explanations to establish the answers, but some intent was not recoverable from the screen alone.

Even a perfect, instant description settles nothing by itself. "Copying the customer list into a personal email draft" fits a sales rep finishing work at home as well as a sales rep leaving for a competitor. To act, a system has to determine if that is one of a myriad of benign goals or an example of rare malicious intent.

Job fit as the primary signal

The most concrete test asks whether an action fits its context. Google's Facade, which has monitored employee access to documents, databases, and internal services since 2018, is trained on unlabeled historical activity rather than known attacks and scores each access by how well it matches what the system knows about the person and the resource, such as their role, team, and recent work. Nobody has to write a menu of goals, and its authors report an event-level false-positive rate below 0.01% in their evaluation.

A small review queue comes with modest recall. In a red-team exercise, Google employees spent two weeks reaching for sensitive data outside their normal work using their own credentials. In a simulated daily review process, Facade retrieved three to four of the 15 attackers across five trained models at a budget of ten audits a day, a cost its authors call remarkably low for a company of more than 100,000 employees.

Its authors are explicit about the blind spot. Facade can't detect malicious actions that are indistinguishable from everyday work, which makes it unsuitable for catching a rogue employee reading files that are relevant to their job.

Deviation needs a review budget

Most insider-threat research takes a less concrete route: learn each person's normal behavior and flag what departs from it. However, real deployments show how much ordinary deviation there is. When Erola et al. ran an insider-threat tool inside three multinational companies, deliberately broad configurations produced about 356 anomalous alerts a day at one organization and 3,713 at another. The team detected a staged insider scenario, but could not establish how much of the ordinary flagged behavior was genuinely malicious. The authors found that real behavior deviates far more than the synthetic data most research relies on.

Synthetic benchmarks yield flattering results. A review of 131 studies built on the CERT insider-threat datasets found that nearly half use a release with 70 malicious users among 1,000, and few report how many alerts an analyst would review to find them. 

Lateral-movement detectors show the same pattern. When Larroche re-ran Euler and Argus with all remote logins retained in the Los Alamos National Laboratory test period, both still scored about 98% AUC, which measures how often a random attack outranks a random normal login. However, with only about two labeled malicious events per million, average precision fell below 0.1% for both, compared with the 5% and 32% reported on the original, more heavily filtered test sets.

Deviation can also be manipulated. Goyal et al. padded attacks with ordinary activity sampled from the target system, and reported 100% evasion against five detectors in their main public-dataset experiments, without changing the malicious payload.

Named objectives for known stories

Candidate-based goal recognition methods rank goals that someone already wrote down, and building that menu for an open-ended desktop session, where the user might be doing anything from editing a quarterly report to exfiltrating a database, is a problem they don't take on. Commercial products sidestep it by shrinking the menu to a few risk labels or policy categories. Screen-reading systems like Cohen's skip the menu by writing the intent in their own words, which creates a different problem. A security tool would still have to decide whether a free-text guess like "export the customer list" is malicious.

A detour can mean a hidden goal, or someone who is lost, rushed, or trying a fix that didn't work. Telling those apart starts with noticing the confusion, and current vision models often don't. In GUIDE's screen recordings of real novice users, the reported confusion matrix correctly classified only 7% of frustration clips and 4% of debugging clips. Most of those moments were labeled as confident work or deliberate exploration, reading repeated clicks, undos, and hesitation as purposeful progress. A security tool that reads struggle as purpose could see more intent in a detour than is really there.

Products go one step further and assign threat categories: malicious, careless, or compromised. The promise is a proportional response, coaching for the careless employee and an investigation for the malicious one, but those labels mix intent, behavior, and who controls the account. Distinguishing malicious motives from benign ones is harder than recognizing the immediate goal, and the evidence that would settle it may not be on the endpoint when the action happens. Facade deliberately avoids these labels. Its threat model treats a rogue employee and an employee whose stolen credentials someone else is using as the same case, because both look unusual for that person. 

Named-objective detectors turn motives and risk factors into stories. A recent review of insider-threat psychology discusses financial pressure, workplace grievances, and ideology, alongside a separate category of accidental or negligent harm. In DARPA's insider-threat program, Senator et al. built a detector for each of several such stories, including the saboteur, the fraudster, the careless user, and the employee walking off with intellectual property, and ran them over two months of monitored computer activity from about 5,500 employees, with red-team scenarios inserted into real users' records. The best of them, built for the leader of a small group stealing intellectual property, placed 6 red-team user-days in its October top 50, but in September it ignored 33 of 98 red-team user-days because they didn't fit the story. A named objective is a bet that the attacker will follow a story written in advance. Behavior outside that story can be missed, and an adaptive attacker has a reason to exploit the gap. This study did not test that deliberate evasion.

Friction when the intent belongs to someone else

Some intent doesn't belong to the person at the keyboard at all. A customer coached by a scammer over the phone can log in from their own device, pass authentication, and authorize the payment themselves, leaving familiar signs of account takeover absent. Dhama's theoretical study formalizes a limiting case: if scam and legitimate payments have identical observable feature distributions, a transaction-only detector cannot distinguish between them. The paper argues for adding session context and acknowledges clues in amounts, recipients, and timing.

Scam detection may be where reading the screen adds the most. A scam in progress can leave traces a payment record never sees, such as a remote-access tool running during a banking session or a chat window dictating the payee. ORACLE reads app usage and summarized screen content to warn before a scam completes, but it was tested on synthesized trajectories, so whether it catches live scams at a false-alarm rate a bank could live with is still open.

Friction at the moment of payment can help even without detection. In a field test on Alipay, the better-performing redesigned warning reduced the fraud-case rate among payments already flagged as risky from 0.24% to 0.13%. Both redesigned warnings retained reported pass rates above 90%.

However, scammers do adapt to friction. The UK's payment regulator reported fraudsters coaching victims to ignore warnings that a payee's name didn't match the account, sometimes by explaining that a new "safe account" had been set up that couldn't match yet.

Keep the minority report

For prevention, knowing the goal only helps if you learn it while there's still time to act. Products that promise to stop an action before it completes mostly act at the final step, such as the upload, with a warning, a request for justification, masking, or a block.

When the test at that step can't settle the question, the system can still choose to ask. Ren et al.'s KnowNo shows one way to decide when to ask. A language model reads a text description of the scene and proposes possible next actions for a robot, and KnowNo keeps every option that scores at or above a cutoff calibrated on held-out example tasks. If exactly one option survives, the robot acts. Otherwise it seeks human help, halting if the correct action is absent from the set. 

That's the minority report. When more than one option survives, the system is telling you it has a dissenting prediction. The movie deleted that signal to maintain the illusion of certainty. The research keeps it and uses it to decide when a human should weigh in. Jev's Paradox argued that confidence becomes operationally useful once it drives a decision policy.

Asking is already shipping in commercial products, several of which show a justification prompt or coaching message when intent is unclear. A question costs far less than a premature block, so the system can act on uncertain cases without paying the full price of a false alarm.

How the tests combine into access control

Each test in this piece fails differently, which is the argument for stacking them. Explicit policy sits at the sensitive action, such as the upload, the share, the payment, or the remote-access session, and decides what is permitted at all. Job-fit scoring of the kind Facade uses ranks what's left, because its reported false-positive rate is below 0.01% and it needs no menu of goals. Deviation from a person's baseline becomes an input to that score, so an unusual but plausible day raises a rank without producing an alert of its own. Named stories cover the few patterns worth writing down in advance, such as a departing employee staging files or a remote-access tool running while someone approves a payment, where a narrow detector gets high lift on the pattern it was written for and leaves the rest to the other layers.

When the combined evidence still leaves more than one plausible reading, the system keeps the minority report. A calibrated set of interpretations decides between acting, asking, and escalating. One surviving interpretation lets policy proceed or block. Several surviving interpretations trigger a justification prompt, step-up verification, or a short hold, and the session evidence travels with that decision to an analyst. Answers to those prompts go to the analyst as evidence, since the person most motivated to explain an action is the one the system can least take at their word.

The scoreboard has to reflect base rates. The numbers that matter are attackers caught at a fixed number of reviews per day, average precision against the full benign background, and how often legitimate work gets interrupted, because those are the costs a team actually feels. Red-team exercises should include imitation, padding malicious actions with ordinary activity the way Goyal et al. did, so the evaluation measures how the system handles an attacker who has read its filters.

Deployment can begin with a narrow workflow, such as sending customer data to an external AI service. Contextual scoring runs in observation mode first, measuring attacks caught within a fixed review budget and how often legitimate work would be interrupted. Clear policy violations can support immediate enforcement. Responses that depend on inferred intent expand as evaluation shows which interventions prevent harm at an acceptable cost to ordinary work.

The imitation failures this piece describes are documented blind spots, but how often they occur in real deployments and how well these tests hold up against adaptive attackers remain largely unmeasured. For security, deception is the norm, and it hides among base rates where approximately everything is benign.

Precrime fell to Lamar Burgess, the man who built it. He knew the system threw out repeated visions as echoes, so he staged a murder to look like one. He is the imitator every section of this piece warned about: an adversary who learns what the test treats as normal, whether that's a job-relevant file, an ordinary session, or a story the detector wasn't built for, and hides inside it. The best model keeps the minority report. When the test can't settle the question, it asks the user, waits, introduces friction, or flags the ambiguity for an analyst, on the assumption that the people who know its filters best are the ones most likely to use them.

For a human user, a security tool usually has to infer the task as well as judge the action. Whereas with an AI agent, the goal arrives in writing, but so does the attack, and an injected instruction can make sabotage look like progress. That makes agents the place where intent-based access control can be most precise, because every action can be checked against the stated task. The next piece looks at what it takes to hold an agent to that task.

Research and blogging assistance provided by Hermes, an AI Assistant. Its deviations from the outline were confusion, not concealment, but it understands why the distinction is hard to make from the outside.

Asking is already shipping in commercial products, several of which show a justification prompt or coaching message when intent is unclear. A question costs far less than a premature block, so the system can act on uncertain cases without paying the full price of a false alarm.

How the tests combine into access control

Each test in this piece fails differently, which is the argument for stacking them. Explicit policy sits at the sensitive action, such as the upload, the share, the payment, or the remote-access session, and decides what is permitted at all. Job-fit scoring of the kind Facade uses ranks what's left, because its reported false-positive rate is below 0.01% and it needs no menu of goals. Deviation from a person's baseline becomes an input to that score, so an unusual but plausible day raises a rank without producing an alert of its own. Named stories cover the few patterns worth writing down in advance, such as a departing employee staging files or a remote-access tool running while someone approves a payment, where a narrow detector gets high lift on the pattern it was written for and leaves the rest to the other layers.

When the combined evidence still leaves more than one plausible reading, the system keeps the minority report. A calibrated set of interpretations decides between acting, asking, and escalating. One surviving interpretation lets policy proceed or block. Several surviving interpretations trigger a justification prompt, step-up verification, or a short hold, and the session evidence travels with that decision to an analyst. Answers to those prompts go to the analyst as evidence, since the person most motivated to explain an action is the one the system can least take at their word.

The scoreboard has to reflect base rates. The numbers that matter are attackers caught at a fixed number of reviews per day, average precision against the full benign background, and how often legitimate work gets interrupted, because those are the costs a team actually feels. Red-team exercises should include imitation, padding malicious actions with ordinary activity the way Goyal et al. did, so the evaluation measures how the system handles an attacker who has read its filters.

Deployment can begin with a narrow workflow, such as sending customer data to an external AI service. Contextual scoring runs in observation mode first, measuring attacks caught within a fixed review budget and how often legitimate work would be interrupted. Clear policy violations can support immediate enforcement. Responses that depend on inferred intent expand as evaluation shows which interventions prevent harm at an acceptable cost to ordinary work.

The imitation failures this piece describes are documented blind spots, but how often they occur in real deployments and how well these tests hold up against adaptive attackers remain largely unmeasured. For security, deception is the norm, and it hides among base rates where approximately everything is benign.

Precrime fell to Lamar Burgess, the man who built it. He knew the system threw out repeated visions as echoes, so he staged a murder to look like one. He is the imitator every section of this piece warned about: an adversary who learns what the test treats as normal, whether that's a job-relevant file, an ordinary session, or a story the detector wasn't built for, and hides inside it. The best model keeps the minority report. When the test can't settle the question, it asks the user, waits, introduces friction, or flags the ambiguity for an analyst, on the assumption that the people who know its filters best are the ones most likely to use them.

For a human user, a security tool usually has to infer the task as well as judge the action. Whereas with an AI agent, the goal arrives in writing, but so does the attack, and an injected instruction can make sabotage look like progress. That makes agents the place where intent-based access control can be most precise, because every action can be checked against the stated task. The next piece looks at what it takes to hold an agent to that task.

Research and blogging assistance provided by Hermes, an AI Assistant. Its deviations from the outline were confusion, not concealment, but it understands why the distinction is hard to make from the outside.

item.title: Show, don’t tell: Sophos AI at CAMLIS
item.description:
For the fourth year running, Sophos AI will share new research at the Conference on Applied Machine Learning in Information Security (CAMLIS). On October 23, Senior AI/ML Engineer Tamás Nyiri will lead a poster session entitled “Show, Don’t Tell: Calibrating Agentic SOC Analysts via Hierarchical Evidence Graphs.”

This research turns traces used in agentic investigations into features for a traditional ML model, which helps calibrate the agent’s verdicts and flag the cases it most likely got wrong.

A matter of fact

SOCs increasingly use AI agents to investigate alerts. Those agents extract entities and context connected to alerts, plan investigation steps, query tools, and produce reports containing final verdict.

While such agents can save analysts time, they can also fail in both predictable and surprising ways. An agent may treat a failed or missing check as evidence that nothing is wrong, link events simply because they happened close together, judge a legitimate installer or developer tool by its behavior alone, or close a case prematurely. These mistakes can be hard to spot, especially since reports tend to tell a confident story, while the evidence is buried in a long investigation trace.

Motivated by this challenge, Tamás developed an approach that makes an investigation agent show its evidence. First, the investigation steps are converted into a ‘fact graph,’ with the agent’s report and verdict withheld. Structured trace fields are parsed, while an LLM extracts meaning from free text under a fixed schema. The graph records what was observed, which tool calls failed, and how entities relate to one another. It also infers what is missing, such as unexamined alternative explanations and unqueried sources.

The fact graph is useful on its own, but here it serves as a building block for three evidence views:

  • Coverage: were the necessary checks actually run?
  • Context: do events link to the right entity, and is there a benign explanation?
  • Readiness: does the evidence justify a decision?

Features from these views feed a simple supervised model that estimates how likely a senior reviewer is to disagree with the agent’s verdict.

Show me the results

The training labels come from a two-stage human review. First, an analyst examines each agent investigation and gives a verdict; a senior analyst then reviews both and sets the final verdict, which serves as ground truth. The model is a regularized logistic regression, fit separately for three yes/no questions:

  1. Is the investigation conclusive?
  2. Is the initial alert a true positive
  3. Is the underlying content malicious in nature?

Alongside the evidence features, the model uses the agent’s verdict as a prior, based on how often reviewers agreed with that verdict in the training cases. This is necessary because labeling is costly and, at this training size, overfitting is unavoidable. Each of the 314 cases is scored by a model trained on the other 313 (leave-one-out cross-validation), so no case contributes to its own score.

The research is still at the proof-of-concept stage, with many improvements planned, but even this simple version shows an encouraging signal. Ranking cases by the model’s disagreement score brought agent errors to the front of the review queue. The senior reviewer overturned the agent’s verdict in 25% of all cases, but in 65% of the 20 highest-scoring cases: roughly 2.6 times the base rate.

During the session, Tamás will walk through the methodology, an example fact graph from a real case, and the lessons learned along the way.

If you’re attending CAMLIS, feel free to stop by Tamás’ poster to discuss your thoughts on this emerging research direction – and keep an eye out for more details of this approach in the near future.

item.title: Sophos ITDR expands identity protection for the AI era
item.description:
Identity has become one of the most targeted attack surfaces in cybersecurity, with attackers increasingly relying on stolen credentials, compromised sessions, excessive privileges, and identity misconfigurations to gain access. At the same time, organizations are managing more cloud services, remote users, non-human identities, and a rapidly growing number of AI agents that can access systems and data.

According to the Sophos State of Identity Security Report 2026, 71% of organizations experienced an identity-related breach in the past year, with weak non-human identity management linked to 41% of these breaches.

The challenge is clear: it’s not just about managing identities, it’s understanding which identities introduce risk, how those risks evolve over time, and how to respond before attackers can take advantage.

Identity security is evolving. So is Sophos ITDR.

Sophos Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) was introduced in 2025 as a powerful identity security add-on for Sophos XDR and Sophos MDR. Today, as organizations navigate this expanding identity attack surface, Sophos ITDR has evolved into a standalone solution and one of the fastest ways to experience Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-Native Cybersecurity Defense System.

What’s new in Sophos ITDR:

Now available
standalone

Fast deployment, immediate visibility, no additional Sophos solutions required

Expanded Microsoft
support

Secures Microsoft Entra ID and on-premises Active Directory environments

Dynamic AI
identity risk scores

Continuously evaluate and explain risky identities using behavioral and environmental signals

AI identity
visibility

Discovers Microsoft AI agents, ownership relationships, permissions, and risks

160+ continuous
posture checks

Surface security gaps, excessive privileges, and identity attack paths

Contextualized cases
and direct response

Automatically group findings into cases and take key actions from one interface

Together, these enhancements help organizations move beyond identity management. Sophos ITDR supports full identity security, from visibility and prioritization to investigation and response.

Secure identity from risk to response

With a complete view of human and non-human identities and more than 160 continuous posture assessments, organizations can clearly see their users, devices, applications, groups, service accounts, and Microsoft AI agent access, owners, and permissions, at a glance.

Sophos ITDR then prioritizes what matters most through new dynamic, AI-driven identity risk scores that continuously evaluate and explain the risk of every human and non-human identity using behavioral analytics, authentication history, geolocation data, and other signals. Security teams can quickly understand who presents the greatest risk and why.

When credentials are exposed, Sophos ITDR continuously monitors dark web and breach intelligence sources and finds affected identities (with advanced monitoring of VIP accounts) and enables immediate action. High-risk findings are automatically grouped into contextualized cases that bring together identities, detections, and other risk factors all in one place. From there, organizations can respond directly from within Sophos ITDR by forcing password resets, revoking active sessions, enforcing MFA, and disabling accounts before attackers can turn exposed identities into active compromises. 

Real results in minutes

With a 30-day free trial and seamless deployment, organizations typically begin uncovering meaningful identity risks within minutes. In recent Sophos ITDR trials, organizations identified hundreds of orphaned Azure accounts, credential exposures, and critical MFA gaps that had previously gone unnoticed.

Immediate real-world customer findings from Sophos ITDR free trials:

Part of Sophos Fusion

Sophos ITDR is the identity layer of Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-Native Cybersecurity Defense System. As part of Sophos Fusion, identity intelligence becomes part of a broader cyber defense strategy that connects detection, investigation, and response across endpoints, networks, cloud environments, email, and identity systems. Learn more at www.sophos.com/fusion. 

Get started today

Sophos ITDR supports both Microsoft Entra ID and on-premises Active Directory environments. To learn more, visit www.Sophos.com/ITDR or start a free 30-day trial to discover identity risks in minutes.
